hours: Wed - Sat 10am to 7pm (installation visible, free entry)

shows.title: Une fenêtre contre le temps (A Window Against Time)
shows.description:
This show closes out Drawing Factory II, a six-month residency that put fifteen artists to work in a shared building at 61 Rue de Richelieu, by moving their output next door into the Drawing Hotel and into Drawing Lab itself. Curator Claire Luna treats "drawing" in its most elastic sense: a line, a gesture, a video, a smell, a piece of furniture, anything that carries the trace of a hand and a period of shared, quiet attention.

Rather than a conventional hang, the works infiltrate the hotel's actual functions — a mood report standing in for the weather on the café television, a strange geological-looking loaf turning up at random on breakfast plates, ants parading across a library shelf, a single guest room made inhabitable for one night by an artist's intervention. The effect is less an exhibition to look at than an atmosphere to notice, built from small disruptions to ordinary hospitality.

The fifteen participants — among them Amélie Barnathan, Tamaris Borrelly, Marguerite Canguilhem, Louise Dumas, Justine Joly, Boryana Petkova and Adji Titus — represent a cross-section of a younger generation of artists trained or based in Paris, most showing publicly for the first time since their residency. It's a modest, unhurried show, and it closes within days, so this is very much a last-chance visit before Drawing Lab turns to its next, more historically-minded project.

shows.title: Virgin Turns (Virages Vierges)
shows.description:
Pauline Curnier Jardin builds immersive, slightly unhinged worlds out of video, fabric sculpture and performance, and this survey at Palais de Tokyo is the biggest showcase of her work to date in France. The title plays on a double meaning: virgins as female bodies loaded with centuries of sanctification and suspicion, saints and sinners at once, and virgin territory as unmapped ground where new stories can take root. Both readings run through the show's tented, womb-like installations and looping video works, where ritual, camp theatrics and documentary footage bleed into each other without much regard for hierarchy.

The centerpiece is a new video installation inspired by a real clandestine cinema discovered in 2004 in tunnels beneath the Trocadéro, practically underneath the museum itself, a detail that gives the whole show a nice sense of digging into buried, dissident histories literally on its own doorstep. Elsewhere, large fabric structures recall crumbling amphitheaters and reliquaries, staging her recurring interest in bodily vulnerability, popular spirituality and the theater of femininity.

Curnier Jardin has been circling these ideas for years in group shows at Palais de Tokyo and in major presentations at Hamburger Bahnhof and elsewhere, but Virgin Turns is her fullest statement yet, and it's being organized in partnership with the Reina Sofía in Madrid, which will host its own version in 2027. It's an odd, immersive, occasionally overwhelming show, well suited to a museum that has always made room for art on the edge of spectacle.

venue.name: Palais de Tokyo
hours: Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun: 12pm to 10pm

shows.title: Les Chiens de Pavlov (Pavlov's Dogs)
shows.description:
Johan Creten has spent nearly forty years reestablishing ceramics as a serious contemporary medium, working his way through studios in Mexico, Rome, Miami and The Hague before settling into La Solfatara, the shared Montreuil studio he keeps with Jean-Michel Othoniel. This new show at Perrotin's Marais space starts from an unusually personal object: a stack of obsolete computer towers inherited from his father, a lifelong devotee of new technology, which Creten piles up like ruins and treats as a monument to a certain kind of faith in progress that has visibly aged.

Around that installation, the exhibition fills out with the vocabulary Creten is best known for: glazed stoneware and bronze creatures, drawings, and recurring figures like his condor and Danaé, cast here in new material or new scale. The title nods to Pavlov's conditioning experiments, and Creten uses it to prod at reflex and automatism, how quickly certain images or objects trigger a response before we've thought about why. A section given over to the seven virtues slows the pace back down, working as counterweight to the show's more anxious, tech-fossil energy.

It's a free, walk-in show and a good entry point into Creten's work if you don't know it: playful in material, but with real unease underneath about memory, obsolescence, and what we choose to keep believing in.

shows.title: Mémoire Matérielle
shows.artist: Gaëlle Choisne, Joana Choumali, Andile Dyalvane, Carla Gueye
shows.description:
Four artists share a conviction that the hand is a form of thinking: this show gathers coil-built ceramics, embroidered photographs, cast and accumulated sculpture, and a room-scale installation of salvaged materials, all bound by processes that take time and leave visible traces of labor. Andile Dyalvane's ceramic vessels carry the scarified surface language of amaXhosa ritual objects; Joana Choumali continues her signature practice of stitching directly into photographic prints, turning embroidery into a slow act of repair and remembrance; Carla Gueye builds sculptural surfaces through touch and accretion; and 2024 Prix Marcel Duchamp laureate Gaëlle Choisne expands the show into installation, working with reclaimed matter tied to Creole and Franco-Haitian histories.

Curated by Azu Nwagbogu and Nkhensani Mkhari, the exhibition takes as its intellectual anchor the Martinican theorist Paulette Nardal's 1930s writing on memory as something built rather than simply inherited — a labor of reconstruction rather than nostalgia. That framework gives the show its throughline: each artist treats craft and material process (clay, thread, cast metal, found objects) as a way of holding onto ancestral and personal history that colonial modernity tried to sever.

Visitors can expect a quietly physical exhibition — heavy with texture, slow to read, and more interested in the residue of making than in finished spectacle. It's a strong choice for anyone curious about how contemporary African and diaspora artists are using traditional hand-craft vocabularies (coiled ceramics, embroidery, assemblage) to make arguments about history and inheritance.

shows.title: Nos géographies intimes (Our Intimate Geographies)
shows.description:
Hervé Yamguen's second solo show at AFIKARIS brings together drawings, paintings, bronze sculpture, and wooden masks built around a single question: what makes up a person beyond what's visible? Yamguen, who is also a poet and a notable within his home chiefdom in Cameroon, treats faces, trees, birds, and hybrid figures as vessels for accumulated experience — places lived in, ancestors carried forward, seasons that mark a body the way they mark a tree.

The bronzes are cast using the lost-wax technique in Foumban, putting an old regional craft in direct conversation with Yamguen's contemporary drawing and painting practice; works on paper and canvas extend into volume and back again, as if the same image kept changing material. Thematically the show leans on Ubuntu philosophy and animist thought — the idea that a person is never separate from ancestors, land, or the non-human world — rather than presenting identity as fixed or singular.

It's a good entry point for anyone interested in contemporary Central African sculpture and drawing that stays close to spoken and sung tradition without illustrating it literally; Yamguen's figures are layered and unresolved by design, closer to accumulation than portraiture.

shows.title: Sfondo
shows.description:
Pauline Bazignan's first solo show at Backslash keeps her long-running dialogue with Italian Renaissance painting but redirects it toward a single, oddly specific target: the landscape behind the Mona Lisa. Rather than copying Leonardo's figure, Bazignan tries to reconstruct the strange background terrain that surrounds her, building the compositions in successive painted layers and then letting water dissolve and drag parts of the pigment away — a controlled-accident process that produces her own version of sfumato, somewhere between appearance and erasure.

The Mona Lisa herself surfaces only faintly across the paintings, more felt than seen, while the horizon and rock formations behind her become the real subject. The show also includes sculptures from Bazignan's recurring series, cast in the same misty blues and earth tones as the paintings, plus an opening diptych inspired by Paolo Uccello's Battle of San Romano that bridges her previous body of work with this new one.

Bazignan trained at the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris and has shown at institutions including the Musée d'Art Moderne de Fontevraud and the Villa Datris Foundation; this is a good show for anyone interested in contemporary painters working through — rather than against — the most over-reproduced image in Western art.

shows.title: Essence
shows.description:
Morgan Courtois works mainly in cast and carved sculpture, often in materials — soap, resin, plaster — that carry a built-in fragility or a suggestion of the body's own softness and impermanence. "Essence" is his second show at Balice Hertling since his 2016 debut there, following a run of institutional presentations that include the Fondation Pernod Ricard and the Centre d'art contemporain Les Capucins.

Courtois's figures tend to hover between the classical and the eroded: torsos, faces, and hands that look excavated or half-dissolved rather than modeled, as if sculpture here is as much about material loss as about form. Given the show's title, expect a body of work that strips its subjects down toward something closer to residue or essence than to finished portraiture.

It's a compact but focused show worth catching for anyone interested in contemporary approaches to figurative sculpture that lean into decay and unstable material rather than permanence.

shows.title: Catching Forms. Wood to Bronze
shows.description:
David Nash has spent five decades working directly with felled and salvaged timber, letting the character of each piece of wood — how it splits, how it dries, its inherent volume — guide the sculpture that emerges. This show tracks a parallel practice he's developed more recently: casting those wood forms into bronze, translating something perishable and organic into something durable.

The pivot point, literally and conceptually, was Inside/Outside (2011), where Nash cast the negative space chainsawed out of a tree stump — turning a void into a solid form. A larger version, Night Form (2026), anchors this exhibition alongside sculptures like the Celtic Column and Cross Column, pieces first developed as wood in his converted-chapel studio in Wales before being reworked and cast. The bronzes carry the memory of their wooden origins in their surfaces, some finished black to mimic charred wood, others taking on green, brown or red patinas that pull them further from their source material.

It's a good entry point into Nash's practice for anyone who knows him primarily as a wood sculptor — the bronzes make the underlying logic of his working method, catching and fixing a form, unusually legible, precisely because the material has changed but the gesture hasn't.

shows.title: Pineta
shows.description:
For twenty years Fabienne Verdier has returned each summer to the Bay of Porto Vecchio in Corsica, and this show is essentially a distillation of that repeated looking. Working in dry pastel for rock and stone and oil pastel for the gnarled pine trunks, she renders the headlands, coves and horizon lines of the coast in spare, almost sculptural marks — drawings that feel closer to carving than mark-making.

The restraint is the point: a single collaged sheet of blue paper stands in for the sea's flatness, and the pastel strokes leave enough white space that the works ask to be read as much through absence as through line. It's a sensory approach to landscape that trades detail for something closer to atmosphere — the scent of resin, the sound of wind through needles — built from a place Verdier clearly knows intimately rather than one she's visiting as a subject.

Verdier's reputation was built on her calligraphic abstraction, developed after years of training in China, and this Corsican series shows that same disciplined, gestural hand turned toward a specific, real landscape rather than pure abstraction — a useful show for seeing how her formal vocabulary adapts when there's an actual place behind it.

shows.title: How Do You Even Sleep At Night?
shows.description:
Wallen Mapondera has built his reputation on sculptural assemblages made from cardboard, packaging and repurposed textiles — materials that carry the economic history of everyday survival in Zimbabwe. This third solo show with the gallery marks a genuine pivot: a body of new paintings that extends his long-running interest in informal trade and state power into a more traditional medium.

The title poses a blunt moral question, and it comes from a personal source — the seizure of goods belonging to the artist's sister, who runs a clothing business, by Zimbabwean authorities acting within the letter of the law. From that specific injury, Mapondera opens onto broader questions about the distance between administrative decisions and the people who absorb their consequences, and about where responsibility lands when an action is legal but experienced as unjust.

It's a show that trades the physical density of his collage work for the more direct address of painting, without losing the social specificity that's always anchored his practice. Worth catching for anyone who's followed his material-based work and wants to see how the same concerns translate onto canvas.

shows.title: MP#06
shows.artist: Jennifer Carlos, Judith Crico, Tavan Esmaili, Léa Pignard, Adrien Viot
shows.description:
This is the graduation show for the sixth cohort of the Fonds Régnier pour la Création's photography mentorship program, run with Agence VU'. Five emerging photographers — Jennifer Carlos, Judith Crico, Tavan Esmaili, Léa Pignard and Adrien Viot — spent nine months in a structured program of mentorship, expert consultations, professional training and collective workshops, and this exhibition is the visible result of that process.

Because it's a mentorship cohort rather than a curated theme show, the work on view spans a real range of approaches and subjects, which makes it a useful snapshot of where younger French documentary and art photography is right now rather than a single argument about it. The gallery also folds in a small selection of prints from the Laurence Régnier private collection, giving visitors a chance to see the five years of the mentorship program (2020–2025) in wider context.

It's a low-key but genuinely useful show for anyone interested in how photography gets professionalized and mentored in France today — less about masterworks than about process, and about a handful of photographers worth watching going forward.

shows.title: Christian Marclay
shows.description:
Christian Marclay has spent decades treating recorded sound as sculptural raw material, and this show turns his attention specifically to the record sleeve — the printed cardboard jacket that protects and advertises a vinyl LP, rather than the disc itself. In a new body of monotypes, he inks paper sleeves and covers in 7", 10" and 12" formats and transfers their surfaces directly onto paper, so that every crease, tear and handling mark left by decades of use becomes part of the final image.

A parallel series called "Oculi" pushes the same material further: Marclay collages vintage sleeves whose circular die-cut windows — originally there to show off the spinning label underneath — become framing devices for isolated fragments of the imagery beneath, a pair of eyes, a mouth, a hand caught mid-gesture. The effect turns cover art designed for quick recognition on a record store shelf into something closer to a cropped, uncanny portrait.

It's a tightly focused, materially inventive show from an artist best known for large-scale sound works and video, here working small and quiet with found ephemera. For anyone who has ever lingered over the graphic design of an old record cover, there's real pleasure in watching Marclay dissect that object down to its printed skin.

venue.name: White Cube
hours: During exhibitions: Tue - Sat 10am to 12:30pm, 1:30pm to 6pm

shows.title: I am Fine: What Woman Wants — Portraits, Figures and Fictions of Femininity
shows.description:
Drawing entirely from the gallery's own collection, this group show gathers a roster of urban-art and street-art-adjacent names — Vhils, YZ, Shepard Fairey, Liu Bolin, Mark Jenkins, André Saraiva, Zevs — alongside painters and sculptors like Cécile Cornet, Rakajoo, Prune Nourry, and FaithXLVII to interrogate how the female figure gets built, worn, and sometimes torn down by the gaze of others. The show's anchor is a Niels "Shoe" Meulman piece: an antique-looking mirror engraved with the phrase "I AM FINE" in calligraphic script, legible only when a viewer's own reflection lines up with the words — so that every visitor becomes, willingly or not, part of the work.

The exhibition moves through a loose narrative arc: it opens on faces (YZ's crowned "Empresses," Erwin Olaf's staged interiors) that stage the tension between woman-as-icon and woman-as-subject, then turns to artists reclaiming their own image — Cornet's scarred, painted bodies passed mother to daughter, Nourry's invented army of "Terracotta Daughters" filling a historical void, Xi Song's papier-mâché spheres built from secondhand books. A second current runs through works that show the female figure being manufactured or erased from outside: Vhils's carved-away faces surfacing from torn advertising posters, Zevs's vandalized fashion billboards, Rakajoo's quietly tense waiting-room portraits.

It's a broad, collection-based survey rather than a single curatorial thesis, but the range is real — from calligraphy and photography to embroidery, carved posters, and street sculpture — and the checklist brings together some genuinely major names in contemporary urban art under a theme with sharper edges than the pun in the title suggests.

shows.title: Au 108 rue Vieille du Temple: A Shared Legacy with Galerie Yvon Lambert
shows.description:
Forty years after Yvon Lambert inaugurated his gallery at 108 rue Vieille du Temple with a Cy Twombly show, David Zwirner marks the anniversary with a group exhibition that treats the address itself as the subject. Lambert ran his program here for nearly three decades before Zwirner took over the space in 2019, and this show threads together thirty-two artists who passed through one or both eras — a rare instance of a gallery building an exhibition around its own site's institutional memory rather than a single artist or theme.

The checklist reads like a survey of postwar conceptual and minimal art crossed with the painters and photographers who gave the program its later range: Twombly, On Kawara, Richard Serra, and Sol LeWitt (who had fifteen solo shows with Lambert) anchor the historical through-line, while Basquiat's "Red Joy," Barbara Kruger's confrontational text pieces, Nan Goldin's photographs, and Bruce Nauman's cast bronze hands broaden it into painting, photography, and sculpture. More recent work by Nathalie du Pasquier and Robert Combas keeps the show from reading purely as archival tribute.

What makes the exhibition worth seeing isn't just the individual pieces but the curatorial premise: wall texts and archival ephemera (show cards, invites designed by LeWitt and Weiner) trace the gallery's own exhibition history at this specific address, turning the show into a compact history of how postwar American art reached Paris audiences through one influential dealer's eye — and how that legacy directly shaped the program that occupies the space today.

shows.title: Les oranges
shows.description:
Elvire Bonduelle returns to Double V's Paris space with "Les oranges," a new solo exhibition of paintings following her recent shows in Marseille and at Art-O-Rama. Bonduelle's work has long circled the textures of everyday domestic and bodily life — food, skin, still life motifs rendered with a loose, saturated hand — and the citrus of the title suggests another close, almost tactile study of ordinary things made strange through color and paint handling.

Based on the works on view, expect bright, high-keyed canvases where fruit, flesh, and interior scenes blur into one another, continuing a practice that has made Bonduelle one of the more distinctive colorists on the current French painting scene. Her pictures tend to hover between figuration and abstraction, holding onto just enough recognizable form — a curve, a rind, a shadow — to keep the eye anchored while the paint itself does something looser and more instinctive.

This is Bonduelle's latest outing with a gallery that has represented her for several years and given her a steady platform across both its Paris and Marseille spaces, making it a good chance to track how her handling of color and everyday subject matter has developed over a run of closely spaced exhibitions.

shows.title: Je suis une économie du désir (I Am an Economy of Desire)
shows.description:
Sarah Tritz fills the gallery with an odd procession: scale models of heavy-duty lorries lined up along the walls, earthenware dinosaurs keeping them company, and sketches of airplanes — drawn on paper deliberately aged and yellowed — raining down from above. Some planes crash, some take off; the trucks and dinosaurs simply keep moving forward. It's a tableau built from mismatched registers of memory, toy-like in scale but heavy with implication.

Tritz has described the dinosaurs in the show as a child's half-remembered composite of an extinct species — a drawing reconstructed from fragments of many "sub-species" that got flattened, in memory, into a single creature called "dinosaur." That slippage between what's recalled and what's real runs through the whole installation: the trucks stand in for the history of commerce and of men, the dinosaurs for a deeper, more mythic history, and somewhere between them, per the artist, sits the unwritten history of women and of children — a category Tritz pointedly suggests may not exist as cleanly as we assume.

The result is less a show about objects than about the "economy" of desire itself: memory, transport, and the small spaces where things are held before they disappear. It's a quietly strange, materially playful body of work from an artist known for treating everyday and toy-scaled objects as vessels for bigger, more ambiguous historical and psychological freight — worth seeing for anyone drawn to sculpture that thinks through miniature form rather than monumental gesture.

shows.title: Predizione Perdizione
shows.description:
João Vilhena continues his Predizione Perdizione series with a third chapter, following presentations in Venice and at the Palais Fesch in Ajaccio. The Paris installment brings together a group of large-scale drawings made in black chalk on grey cardboard, a deliberately humble, matte medium that Vilhena has made his signature over the past decade.

The drawings work through fragments of historical imagery — figures, monuments, scenes that read as excavated from an archive of collective memory — and set them against the artist's own contemporary anxieties. The result is less a narrative than a mood: a slow-burning meditation on prediction and loss (the title translates roughly as "prediction, perdition") that treats drawing as a way of processing what feels historically inevitable.

Vilhena works at a scale that pushes the intimacy of chalk drawing toward something closer to history painting, and the grey cardboard support keeps the palette almost monochrome, all the more dramatic for its restraint. It's a compact, focused show, well suited to a first look at an artist whose vocabulary of stark figuration and worn materials is gaining international attention.

shows.title: Arrière-train fantôme (Ghost Rump)
shows.description:
Marie Losier is best known internationally as a filmmaker — her portraits of outsider musicians and performers (Genesis P-Orridge, Guy Maddin's circle, the duo Arlt) have played festivals worldwide — but this show turns to the drawing, collage, and textile work that runs alongside her films. Pen, watercolor, and collage on paper sit next to sewn and screen-printed fabric pieces, all made with the same restless, handmade energy as her moving-image work.

The pieces on view read like stills pulled from an imaginary film: costumed figures, fetish objects, and fairground imagery rendered in loose, confident line and wet color. Losier has described her practice as one long act of mythologizing the people around her — friends, lovers, chosen family — turning them into recurring characters in a private cosmology, and that same impulse animates the works here, several of which involve close collaborators like the musician Sing Sing (of the band Arlt).

It's a modest-scaled, intimate show, heavy on paper and fabric rather than spectacle, and it rewards close looking — the kind of exhibition where the wall texts (Losier's own writing is characteristically playful and strange) are as worth reading as the images are worth studying.

shows.title: Pluie Fossile
shows.description:
Julien Discrit works at the intersection of stone and data in this show, carving marble the way sculptors have for millennia while feeding it content generated by algorithms and old film scripts. The title, "Fossil Rain," sets the tone: this is an exhibition about how memory gets deposited, layer by layer, in materials that outlast the people who made them.

The centerpiece is a series called Engrammes — marble slabs engraved with fragmentary sentences that read like diary entries or half-remembered dreams ("the smell comes back on the first street, everything's smaller than before"). Discrit calls them "engrams," borrowing the neuroscience term for a physical trace of memory in the brain, and here that trace becomes literal: words cut into stone, permanent where memory itself is not. Alongside them are the sculptural Embrace works, softly rounded marble forms that read as abstracted gestures of holding on.

A parallel body of work, Tears in Rain, takes its title from the Blade Runner replicant monologue about memories "lost like tears in rain," and generates chromatographic ink patterns on silica plates — each one named for a fictional life invented by an algorithm, its supposed key memories plotted as points on an invisible grid. It's a strange, poetic pairing: the oldest sculptural material there is, marked by the newest tools for manufacturing false histories. The show asks what happens to memory when both stone and software can be made to hold it.

shows.title: Glade / Clairière
shows.description:
Wolfgang Tillmans returns to Galerie Chantal Crousel a year after his sprawling Centre Pompidou retrospective closed, and after a year spent as a visiting professor at the Beaux-Arts de Paris. Glade / Clairière is built around a motif the gallery describes as central to his recent work: the line, sometimes drawn and deliberate, sometimes found in the world and simply recorded, running through his photographs as a thread between control and chance.

Tillmans has spent over three decades refusing to settle into a single photographic register — club culture and portraiture sit alongside still lifes, astronomical images, and near-abstractions made through direct manipulation of photographic paper — and this show continues that restlessness rather than resolving it. Expect large-scale prints alongside more intimate works, installed in the loose, non-hierarchical hang that has become one of his own signatures as much as any single image.

As the first photographer and first non-British artist to win the Turner Prize, and with major surveys behind him at Tate, MoMA, and now the Pompidou, Tillmans hardly needs introduction — but a gallery show like this one, scaled to a single space rather than a museum floor, is where his eye for sequencing and juxtaposition is easiest to see up close.

shows.title: Les objecteurs (The Objectors)
shows.description:
Sixty years ago the critic Alain Jouffroy staged a three-gallery Paris event called "Les Objecteurs," pulling together Arman, Tetsumi Kudo, Daniel Pommereulle, Jean-Pierre Raynaud, and Daniel Spoerri under a shared idea: that everyday objects, rather than paint or bronze, could carry thought itself, functioning as provocations rather than as sculpture or parody-painting. Galerie Christophe Gaillard restages that premise for its own space, pairing historical works by Kudo and Pommereulle with a wider group spanning several generations of French object-based art.

The show adds artists of the confirmed postwar generation — Pierre Ardouvin, Eric Baudart, Anita Molinero — whose practices pick up Jouffroy's original argument in different registers: Molinero's scorched and melted industrial plastics (roadside bins, car parts, foam) read the built environment's castoffs as a form of social diagnosis, while Baudart's spare rearrangements of ordinary objects quietly destabilize how familiar things are perceived. A younger generation, represented by David Douard and Mimosa Echard, pushes the object further toward hybrid, almost organic territory — assemblages that mix street debris, technology, and biological or botanical material until the categories blur.

It's a smart piece of historical restaging rather than a straightforward group show: less about any single artist than about tracing a sixty-year lineage of French artists who treat the object, not the image, as the basic unit of thought. Kudo's boxed, dice-like symbolic objects and Pommereulle's charged combinations of blades and found forms anchor the show in its 1960s origins, while the contemporary works make the case that the "objector" impulse never really went away.

shows.title: le flâneur
shows.description:
Jacques Villeglé (1926–2022) made a career out of walking Paris and peeling advertising posters straight off the walls, then presenting the torn, layered, weather-beaten results as finished works — the "affiches lacérées" that made him one of the founding figures of Nouveau Réalisme. "le flâneur" leans into that identity: the show is built around the idea of the artist as urban wanderer, collecting the city's accidental collages rather than inventing his own compositions.

The works on view are named, as Villeglé always named them, for the streets and dates where he tore them down — a poster lifted from the Rue du Théâtre in January 1961, stickers pulled from the Boulevard Saint-Martin in 1978, layers gathered on the Rue du Temple and the Rue Claude Vellefaux. Seen together, they read as a kind of alternative cartography of postwar Paris, each sheet carrying the overlapping graphic noise — typography, color, tears, glue — of whatever campaigns and slogans happened to compete for that particular wall.

There's a deceptively simple pleasure in these pieces: they look like abstraction, but every mark in them was made by someone else, and Villeglé's only intervention was choosing where to cut. Decades on, they still feel like some of the freshest, least mannered gestures to come out of that generation of French art, and this focused hang is a good primer on why he's remained a reference point for artists working with appropriation and the urban surface.

shows.title: Trafic – Hommage à Peter Stämpfli
shows.artist: Eulàlia Grau, Peter Halley, Emanuel Proweller, Daniel Spoerri, Peter Stämpfli, Jacques Villeglé
shows.description:
This group show at the gallery's 33 Rue de Seine space pays tribute to Peter Stämpfli, the Swiss painter best known for his hyperreal, cropped close-ups of tires and racing-car bodywork, by putting him in dialogue with other artists who have made speed, circulation and the imagery of the road part of their vocabulary. It's a loose but coherent premise: traffic as both literal subject and a metaphor for how images and objects move and collide.

Alongside Stämpfli's own tightly rendered tire and car paintings, the show brings in Daniel Spoerri's object-based assemblages, Peter Halley's hard-edged geometric abstractions (themselves indebted to circuitry and infrastructure imagery), Emanuel Proweller's mid-century abstraction, Eulàlia Grau's collage-based social critique, and Jacques Villeglé's torn-poster works — a fitting overlap with his concurrent solo show at the gallery's other space nearby.

It's an unusual pairing of generations and geographies, held together less by shared style than by a common interest in the urban object as raw material, and it gives Stämpfli — a figure sometimes overshadowed by his American Pop contemporaries — a chance to be seen in a wider, more international context of postwar art dealing with mechanization and speed.

shows.title: La Mue
shows.description:
Tessa Mars is a Haitian painter whose work has long circled around a recurring alter ego, Manman Zombi, through whom she explores self-image, Vodou cosmology and the layered colonial and postcolonial history written onto Haitian bodies and land. "La Mue" — literally "the molt" or "the shedding" — points to a show built around transformation: the shedding of skin, of imposed identity, of inherited narrative.

Given the title and Mars's established visual language, expect paintings that stage the body mid-transition, using the vivid color and flattened, folkloric figuration she's known for to suggest metamorphosis rather than a fixed, single self-portrait. Her work consistently treats the personal and the political as inseparable, using her own image as a site where questions of gender, race and national history get worked out in paint.

This is Galerie Imane Farès continuing a program built around artists from the Caribbean, Middle East and African diaspora, and Tessa Mars's first solo outing with the gallery — a good introduction to an artist whose reputation has been building steadily since her early exhibitions in Port-au-Prince and the Caribbean biennial circuit.

shows.title: Au fil de l'eau
shows.description:
Elizabeth Garouste has spent four decades refusing to sit still inside the category of "designer," even though her Barbare chair with the late Mattia Bonetti became one of the defining objects of 1980s French design. Since going solo she's leaned harder into a personal, almost folkloric visual language built from masks, hand-worked bronze and iron, textiles and drawing. This second solo show with Ketabi Bourdet gathers new work around water — the sea, its creatures, its endless capacity for transformation.

Expect the full range of her practice in one room: sculptural furniture and lighting alongside masks built up from plaster bandaging, wrought-iron consoles and mirrors, tapestries, and the loose, naive-inflected drawings she treats as a kind of daily notation. Her forms — heads, faces, animal-hybrid creatures — sit somewhere between art brut and decorative art, refusing the line the market usually tries to draw between the two.

At nearly eighty, Garouste shows no sign of repeating herself, and this gallery — which pairs contemporary art with historically significant design — is a fitting home for work that has always insisted the two were never really separate. Given the show's marine theme, it should read as looser and more atmospheric than her furniture-focused outings, closer to an installation than a showroom.

shows.title: Robert Filliou: Une histoire chuchotée de l'art
shows.description:
Peter Freeman, Inc., which has represented the estate of Robert Filliou for years, turns its Paris gallery over to a survey of the French Fluxus artist's deceptively modest, endlessly inventive work. Filliou (1926–1987) spent his career arguing that art should be indistinguishable from play, gift, and everyday gesture, and the works gathered here — hinged wooden panels of layered drawing under colored acetate, pastel works on paper, silkscreen multiples, and small assembled sculptures — show him working that idea out across drawing, printmaking, and object-making.

Pieces like "Galerie légitime," a wearable, pocket-sized gallery Filliou first staged on the streets of Paris in the 1960s, and "Hand Show," a box of silkscreened prints made with photographer Scott Hyde, reflect his lifelong suspicion of the gallery as the only legitimate site for art. Even the framed and vitrine-bound works on view keep something of that itinerant, DIY spirit — colored film layered over photographs, cardboard and paper hinged together, editions produced with small presses in Düsseldorf and elsewhere.

The show's French title, which translates roughly as "a whispered history of art," captures Filliou's own tone: playful, understated, allergic to grand pronouncements even when making serious points about value, authorship, and what counts as art. For anyone who only knows Fluxus through its noisier figures, this is a good place to recalibrate around one of its gentlest and most philosophically rigorous voices.

shows.title: Anthem
shows.description:
Anthem is Yasuko Hirano's first exhibition with galerie frank elbaz, bringing together recent abstract paintings built from oil, plaster and glue worked into canvas over wooden panels. The surfaces are thick and worked-over, with the plaster giving the paint a chalky, excavated quality — closer to a wall that's been through several rounds of repair than a conventional painted canvas.

Hirano's abstraction keeps circling back to memory, repetition and mental landscape rather than pure formal concerns; the paintings read as records of returning to the same gesture or mark again and again, each pass slightly different from the last. That repetition-as-renewal idea is central to how she talks about her own process — treating painting not as a way of preserving something fixed from the past but as a live encounter that keeps producing new time with each iteration.

For a first Paris gallery show, Anthem is a strong, cohesive introduction: the palette stays close and earthbound, the surfaces reward close viewing, and the whole body of work has the patient, accretive feel of an artist who has been refining a single idea carefully rather than chasing variety.

shows.title: Earth and Sky
shows.description:
Sungi Mlengeya's first monographic exhibition in France arrives as an extension of a signature approach: figures rendered in warm, richly modeled brown tones that seem to float free of any background, the white of the raw canvas standing in for space itself. Bodies emerge mid-gesture, limbs and torsos caught in movement, with everything extraneous around them simply left unpainted.

Titled Earth and Sky, the new body of work turns toward questions of continuity, how a life persists past the point of loss, through memory, inheritance and influence passed between generations. It's a quieter, more reflective register than pure portraiture, using the same pared-back visual language the Tanzanian artist has built her reputation on to think about what remains when someone is gone.

The absence of setting is the whole point: without floor, wall or horizon to anchor them, Mlengeya's figures read as archetypal rather than particular, standing in for a broader meditation on transmission and legacy rather than any single story.

shows.title: We Cannot Stop the Birds of Misfortune From Flying Over Our Heads, But Perhaps We Can Stop Them From Nesting There
shows.description:
Qi Zhuo's new solo show takes its title from a well-worn Chinese proverb about misfortune, but treats the phrase less as consolation than as a working method, a way of handling materials, history and the body without pretending bad luck can be avoided altogether. The works on view, including the bulbous, taut Bubble-Game paintings and the more precarious Balancing Ball pieces, translate that idea into forms that look perpetually on the verge of losing their composure.

There's a tension throughout between control and collapse: surfaces stretched tight, rounded volumes that seem inflated to their limit, objects balanced in ways that look temporary rather than resolved. It's a physical, almost bodily vocabulary, closer to sculpture-as-tension than to straightforward object-making.

Staged at the gallery's second Paris space on rue Chapon, opened in 2023 to expand its program, the show gives Zhuo's restless, unresolved forms room to breathe on their own rather than sharing the spotlight with a second artist.

shows.title: Les Commensaux
shows.description:
José Loureiro's third solo show at the gallery centers on a new series of oils on canvas and paper that stage odd, half-organic forms in perpetual friction with one another. Bodies that read as humanoid one moment and purely abstract the next crowd the picture plane, bumping, merging and pulling apart in compositions that never quite settle into a single register.

The title, "Les Commensaux" (dinner companions), plays on the double life of the French word "table": both a piece of furniture and the site of shared meals. Recurring motifs of toothy little mouths, cutlery-like sticks, and tubular polychrome forms that seem to dissolve at one end tie the paintings to ideas of eating, hosting and coexistence, sometimes convivial, sometimes closer to friction or predation. It's a loud, heterogeneous body of work, deliberately mixing smooth hard-edged passages with loose, expressive brushwork, geometry with gesture.

Loureiro, a major figure in Portuguese painting who recently had a large-scale retrospective spread across three floors of the Frac Grand Large in Dunkirk, has spent decades pushing a minimalist grid vocabulary toward increasingly strange, animate territory; Les Commensaux continues that trajectory, treating heterogeneity itself as the subject rather than a stylistic tic.

shows.title: Ferdinandea
shows.description:
Clément Cogitore's first solo exhibition with the gallery takes its name from a phantom island: Ferdinandea, a volcanic outcrop that briefly surfaced off Sicily in 1831 before sinking back under the Mediterranean, claimed and contested by multiple nations in the few months it existed above water. It's a perfect Cogitore subject, a place that is simultaneously historical fact and geological rumor, and the works on view (grouped under titles like Incertitudes, Vigilances, Cendres and Prémonitions) treat that instability as their organizing logic.

Cogitore, better known to many for his film and video work exploring ritual, belief and contested territory, brings the same interests to these object-based pieces: a fascination with thresholds, half-documented events, and the way collective anxiety attaches itself to unstable ground. The show follows presentations of the same body of work at Madre in Naples and Mucem in Marseille, arriving in Paris as the exhibition's title suggests: an island that keeps reappearing under different institutional skies.

It's a tightly focused solo debut rather than a survey, built around a single mythic hook, and it rewards viewers willing to sit with ambiguity: nothing here resolves into a clean historical account, and that unresolve is the point.

shows.title: Summer Sun: Open my Heart
shows.description:
Robert Kushner has spent decades folding botanical imagery into paintings that refuse to sit quietly within either abstraction or decoration, and this new solo show brings together twelve works made between 2019 and 2025, most on Japanese paper, one on canvas, all built around flowers rendered with a gilded, pattern-heavy exuberance. Chrysanthemums, sunflowers, asters and celosia appear less as botanical illustration than as vehicles for pure visual pleasure: saturated color, metallic ground, and a compositional looseness that owes as much to textile and screen painting traditions as to still life.

Kushner emerged from the Pattern and Decoration movement of the 1970s, and this body of work reads as a mature, confident continuation of that project's core argument, that pattern and ornament are legitimate, serious painting subjects rather than a lesser, merely decorative mode. The Japanese paper support matters here too, its absorbency and texture pulling the pigment into soft, bloom-like edges that a canvas wouldn't produce.

It's a warm, generous show, unapologetically about beauty and abundance, arriving as flowers in late summer and early autumn: chrysanthemums and asters that mark the turn of the season, painted with the same gilded intensity Kushner brings to everything he touches.

shows.title: Mémoires
shows.description:
Sergey Kononov paints quiet, close-cropped scenes of solitude and intimacy, faces and figures rendered in grainy, ochre-warm light that deliberately evokes the texture of old film stock. Mémoires (memories) gathers a new body of work from the Odesa-born, Paris-based painter, who trained at the École des Beaux-Arts de Paris and has spent the past decade refining a soft-focus realist style that sits somewhere between icon painting and Balthus.

The paintings work by withholding as much as they show: subjects are often caught mid-gesture, eyes closed or turned away, hair falling across faces, so that the emotional charge comes from atmosphere and light rather than legible narrative or expression. Kononov has spoken about wanting to recreate the grain and warmth of old film in paint, and that nostalgic, slightly hazy quality gives even contemporary subjects a sense of half-remembered distance, appropriate for a show explicitly framed around memory.

It's an intimate, unhurried body of work, more invested in mood and tenderness than incident, and it continues a run of gallery and institutional recognition for an artist whose paintings favor quiet accumulation of feeling over drama.

shows.title: la soustraite
shows.description:
Gyan Panchal works with objects he pulls out of recycling centers and reuse depots — pieces of plastic, foam, fabric, wood, "cooked by the sun" as the gallery text puts it — and reworks them through a slow, deliberate sequence of washing, cutting, wearing down, repainting and recombining. Nothing is polished into something new; the sculptures keep the traces of what they used to be while shifting into something closer to abstraction. la soustraite (roughly, "the one subtracted" or "the removed") names that process of withdrawal as a method: taking things apart and away rather than adding to them.

The exhibition follows Panchal's recent run of solo shows in France (Angle centre d'art contemporain, Treignac Project, Alea–Artagon) and his 2019 survey at the MAMC+ in Saint-Étienne, and continues the vocabulary he's built over two decades — object, threshold, and a kind of contemporary asceticism that resists the speed of consumption and extraction. It's a quiet, materially exacting show, more about sustained looking than spectacle, and rewards slowing down in front of single objects rather than moving quickly through the space.

Panchal's work sits in major French public collections (Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, Centre Pompidou, several FRACs) as well as at Lafayette Anticipations, and this is his return to Marcelle Alix, the gallery that has represented him for years.

shows.title: Travessia
shows.description:
Patricia Leite paints skies, horizons and half-remembered fragments of landscape — a dawn, a silhouetted branch, an abandoned lounge chair — built up in thin, glowing layers of diluted oil paint that give even her plainest compositions a strange inner light. Travessia (Crossing) brings new paintings made this year, including Minguante (Waning), Travessia II and a view of Paris itself, Nuvem rosa de Paris (The Pink Cloud of Paris), alongside a painting of the Chapel of the Rosary in Vence.

Leite trained through Brazil's early-1980s return-to-painting movement, absorbed and then set aside influences from Klee to Barnett Newman, and spent years developing a personal language centered on color as an emotional signal rather than description — moons, birds and stars appear at the edges of her compositions rather than the center, and the horizon line does most of the structural work. It's an unusually lyrical, unhurried kind of painting, closer to memory than observation, and this is a good showcase for a Brazilian painter whose work is still not widely seen in Paris.

The show opens on the gallery's Place des Vosges location, a fitting setting given the essay accompanying the show explicitly connects Leite's suspended, involuntary-memory way of seeing to Proust.

shows.title: Vie des Formes
shows.description:
Timed to Paris Design Week and AlUla's cultural season in Paris, Vie des Formes puts furniture, sculpture, video and hybrid objects from AlUla's design-residency program in dialogue with works from the Fondation's own collection (Fonds de dotation Famille Moulin). The premise is a blurred line between art and design: some pieces rework craft and vernacular forms, others use natural or recycled materials, and others borrow and subvert the look of industrial production.

The participant list is wide-ranging — Meriem Bennani, Katinka Bock, Camille Blatrix, Matthew Angelo Harrison, Lydia Ourahmane and Mathieu Mercier are shown alongside AlUla-affiliated designers and studios like Altin Studio, bahraini—danish, and Studio ThusThat — which makes for a show about circulation and hybridity as much as about any single medium. Expect an installation that's meant to be handled and lived with rather than viewed at a distance, backed by a week of talks, a solar-powered sound performance, and family workshops.

It's a short run — five days, tied tightly to the design-week calendar — so it functions more as an event-exhibition than a conventional gallery hang, and is worth planning around if you're interested in where contemporary art and design collecting overlap.

shows.title: Aux origines de l'abstraction, 1962-1968
shows.description:
This is an origin story told backwards. Kim Guiline (1936–2021) spent the decades after the mid-1970s refining a signature language of near-monochrome canvases — black, white, or a single primary color, animated only by repetitive raised brushstrokes and a cruciform void running through the surface. This show skips past that mature, tightly theorized body of work to look at what came before it: the formative decade between 1962 and 1968, when the Korean-born, Paris-trained painter was still working his way toward that reduction.

The paintings on view trace a fast unraveling of representation. Early landscapes with heavy impasto give way, by 1963, to flattened, schematic panoramas indebted to late Braque; by 1967 the referents disappear altogether, replaced by bold juxtaposed color planes, geometric bands, and hard-edged compositions that flirt with both Poliakoff's lyricism and the American hard-edge and minimalist painting Guiline encountered in Paris in the late 1960s.

It's a rarely-seen chapter — curated with the input of Musée Cernuschi's Maël Bellec — that reframes Guiline's later, more austere paintings not as a sudden signature style but as the endpoint of a genuine period of searching, essential to understanding how he arrived at the reductive vocabulary for which he's now best known.

shows.title: Carnets ouverts
shows.description:
Joanne Boyer's paintings are built out of light and shadow — figures, landscapes, and architecture emerging from pools of darkness in a way that owes an obvious debt to Caravaggio and Goya. Carnets ouverts (Open Notebooks) steps away from those finished paintings to show the works on paper underneath: gouaches and drawings, small in scale, more exposed in gesture.

Born in 1990 in Versailles, Boyer draws from a personal bestiary of ruined landscapes, forests, sirens, satyrs, and knights, mixed in with unmistakably contemporary details — a coexistence of timelines she doesn't try to resolve into a single narrative. On paper, that vocabulary becomes looser and more immediate: motifs get tried, repeated, abandoned, and picked up again, less as sketches for future paintings than as an autonomous, ongoing record of how her images form.

Shown together for the first time, these sheets offer an unusually intimate way into Boyer's practice — not the polished result but the circulation of ideas that feeds it.

shows.title: La Dolce Vista
shows.description:
Claude Nori has spent half a century photographing summer as a state of mind as much as a season — sunlit bodies on Italian and French beaches, teenagers loitering in the heat, the loose, affectionate intimacy of the Mediterranean everyday. A key figure of the "Photographie Subjective" movement he helped found in the 1970s, Nori works in a warm, unposed, snapshot-adjacent register that treats color and light as emotional material rather than just documentary fact.

La Dolce Vista, opening with the artist present, promises more of that sensibility: a title that puns on la dolce vita while keeping the photographer's gaze — vista — front and center. Expect the loose-limbed, nostalgic romanticism that has made Nori a reference point for a generation of younger photographers working in saturated color.
